analysis.one_liner: Rolls back most post-2008 Wall Street regulations, including bank trading limits and the consumer protection bureau.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Financial CHOICE Act 233-186 on June 8, 2017, with every voting Republican in favor, but the Senate Banking Committee never voted on it and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the Dodd-Frank Act, the set of laws passed after the 2008 financial crisis. It would let banks with a 10% capital ratio opt out of nearly all federal financial regulation, repeal the Volcker Rule ban on banks trading for their own profit, and end the government's special process for winding down failing giant banks. It would also gut the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: renaming it, cutting off its independent funding, ending its supervision of financial firms, and removing its authority over payday loans and forced-arbitration clauses.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and financial firms gain the most. A bank that keeps a 10% capital-to-assets ratio could exempt itself from virtually all federal capital, liquidity, and supervisory rules; the Volcker Rule ban on banks' own speculative trading would be repealed; the FDIC's authority to liquidate a failing giant bank would be replaced with bankruptcy court procedures; and the 'too big to fail' designations of nonbank financial firms would be wiped out retroactively. Payday and vehicle-title lenders would be freed from the consumer bureau's jurisdiction. Broker-dealers, credit rating agencies, and private equity funds would lose liability exposure and registration requirements, and publicly traded companies would shed disclosure rules on conflict minerals, mine safety, and executive pay votes.

how_it_helps.text: A banking organization with an average leverage ratio of at least 10% could elect to be exempt from any federal capital or liquidity requirements, supervisory objections to its capital distributions, and other specified federal rules.
The bill repeals the Volcker Rule, which prohibits banks from proprietary trading and from certain relationships with hedge funds and private equity funds.
It repeals the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority for failing financial institutions and repeals the FDIC's authority to guarantee bank debt during severe economic distress.

It eliminates the Financial Stability Oversight Council's authority to designate non-bank financial institutions and financial market utilities as systemically important, and retroactively repeals previous designations.

It converts the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau into a 'Consumer Law Enforcement Agency' that is subject to congressional appropriations, loses its supervisory and examination authority over financial institutions, and is barred from taking action against payday loans, vehicle-title loans, or similar small-dollar credit, and from restricting mandatory pre-dispute arbitration.
It nullifies the Department of Labor's 2016 fiduciary rule, which required retirement-account advisers to meet standards of impartial conduct.

It repeals Durbin Amendment limits on debit card processing fees charged to retailers, and repeals Dodd-Frank disclosure requirements for conflict minerals, mine safety, and payments to foreign governments.

It also contains narrower provisions that ease rules on smaller institutions, such as escrow exemptions for loans held by creditors with up to $10 billion in assets and reduced reporting for well-capitalized community banks.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost through weaker enforcement against deceptive and abusive lending, the loss of the consumer bureau's supervision of banks and its authority over payday loans, and the reinstatement of forced-arbitration clauses that block class actions. Retailers and their customers would face higher debit card fees with the Durbin Amendment repeal. Taxpayers would carry more risk of absorbing losses in a crisis, since the FDIC's resolution authority for failing giant banks and its bank-debt guarantee authority would be repealed and large banks could opt out of capital and liquidity rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own title, 'Ending Too Big to Fail and Bank Bailouts,' would repeal the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority — the mechanism created after 2008 to unwind failing giant banks without taxpayer bailout — and replace it with bankruptcy procedures whose workability for large complex financial firms was contested.

Allowing banks to opt out of virtually all capital, liquidity, and supervisory rules based on a single 10% leverage ratio would leave less margin for the risk-weighted analysis that regulators use to judge whether banks are actually safe.

Stripping the consumer agency of supervisory and examination authority means it could only sue after harm occurred, rather than detect problems by examining firms' records; eliminating its authority over payday and vehicle-title loans removes oversight of products associated with high-cost repeat borrowing.

The strongest good-faith case for the bill was accountability and relief: Dodd-Frank compliance costs fell heavily on community banks, the consumer bureau was funded outside the appropriations process and led by a single director removable only for cause, and the bill's capital election was conditioned on a high capital standard so only well-capitalized banks could use it. The bill also raised SEC civil penalties in some respects, which supporters cited as 'holding Wall Street accountable.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes real but modest relief for community banks and small-company fundraising with a sweeping rollback of post-2008 safeguards on the largest institutions. The relief provisions are the easier part to defend; the core — deregulating systemically large banks, ending the FDIC resolution authority, and defanging the consumer bureau — would shift risk toward taxpayers and consumers in exchange for higher bank profitability. On balance the costs outweigh the benefits, and the Senate never took the bill up.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a nearly party-line vote, but after arriving in the Senate it got referred to the Banking Committee and only a hearing was ever held — no committee vote, no floor vote — and it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported on May 4, 2017, by a 34-26 vote, and it was reported amended on May 25.
Eight other House committees were discharged from further consideration so the bill could move to the floor, where a rule allowing limited debate and specified amendments was adopted on June 7, 2017.
The House passed the bill on June 8, 2017, by a vote of 233-186, with 233 of 237 Republicans voting yes, 1 voting no, and 0 of 193 Democrats voting yes.

The Senate received the bill on June 12, 2017, referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the committee held a hearing on July 13, 2017 — its last recorded action before the Congress ended.
Under Senate practice, a bill that a committee never reports cannot get a floor vote; the Banking Committee never ordered a markup or vote on H.R. 10, so it never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers, who kept the Dodd-Frank safeguards — the FDIC resolution authority, the Volcker Rule, and a consumer bureau with supervisory power — that the bill would have repealed. Large banks and financial firms lost their best chance in that Congress at broad deregulation, though some of its themes resurfaced in later narrower bills.

for.name: Jeb Hensarling
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through his committee, which held hearings, marked it up, and reported it amended by a 34-26 vote.

for.name: 233 of 237 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing all but 1 of the 233 votes in favor.

for.name: 40 House Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for rolling back Dodd-Frank and urged Congress to pass the bill, making it an administration priority.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to his committee and held only a hearing; never brought it to a committee vote or reported it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which under Senate practice required a committee report first.

against.name: 185 of 193 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, unanimously opposing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The fight split almost exactly by party: on the House floor, 233 of 237 Republicans voted yes and 0 of 193 Democrats did, and all 40 cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.note: The bill's capital election would let banks meeting a 10% leverage ratio exempt themselves from virtually all federal capital, liquidity, and supervisory rules, and it repeals the Volcker trading ban, the FDIC resolution authority for failing giant banks, and 'too big to fail' designations. Its benefit is the industry's freed-up capital and trading profits; the offsetting risk — more bailouts and more fragile banks — falls on taxpayers and depositors.

The bill removes the consumer agency's authority over payday loans, vehicle-title loans, and other similar small-dollar credit entirely. These lenders profit from high-cost repeat borrowing that the consumer bureau was created to police.

industries.industry: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and private equity funds
industries.note: The bill nullifies the Labor Department's fiduciary rule for retirement advisers, exempts private equity fund advisers from Investment Advisers Act registration, and limits SEC enforcement tools such as penalty conditions and disqualification of repeat violators. Lower compliance and liability costs for the industry come at the expense of investor protections.

The bill repeals rating-agency attestations of independence, expert liability for ratings, and mandatory annual examinations. These are the same safeguards added after agencies rated failed mortgage securities AAA before the 2008 crisis.

It repeals disclosure rules on conflict minerals, mine safety, and payments to foreign governments, lets companies skip 'say-on-pay' votes absent material pay changes, and raises the thresholds at which small companies must register with the SEC.

The bill gives smaller institutions genuine relief — escrow exemptions, reduced reporting, examination fairness standards — which runs alongside borrowers' interest in credit access. But the bill's headline off-ramp (Title VI) and bailout repeal mainly serve the largest firms, so community banks are incidental beneficiaries of a bill built around Wall Street deregulation.

Repealing the Durbin Amendment's debit-card fee caps would have let banks charge retailers more on every debit transaction, costs likely passed into prices. Retailers' interest in keeping the caps ran alongside consumers'.
